Americans are worried about inflation.

US consumer median 1-year ahead inflation expectations jumped +0.3 percentage points in September, to 3.9%, their highest level since May 2023.

This figure has risen +0.9 percentage points since February.

Over the next year, consumers expect gasoline prices to increase +4.8%, food prices to rise +5.5%, medical costs to surge +9.2%, the price of a college education to jump +7.5%, and rent prices to rise +6.8%.

1-year inflation expectations have now been at or above 3.0% for 22 consecutive months.

Meanwhile, 3-year inflation expectations rose +0.1 percentage point last month, to 3.3%, the highest level since June 2022.

Consumers are bracing for a prolonged period of higher prices.

11/11 — BANKS ARE NEXT

If your bank analyst doesn't understand Stripe's growth numbers, crypto's evolving regulatory guardrails and applications, and the speed of agentic commerce, how can they accurately value the future of banking?

Ask software analysts what they missed a year ago. Ask memory analysts what they missed 15 months ago.

The common mistake? Underestimating the SPEED of AI-driven change.

Markets don't wait for earnings to collapse. They reprice the future first.

Banks are next.

10/10 — BANKPOCALYPSE

My thesis is not that banks vanish.

It's that their historical share of economic activity, customer relationships and fee income is no longer guaranteed and those rediculous spreads (time and fees) are reduced through competition of speed and efficiency.

Stripe shows how AI, crypto and tokenization can move financial services into software.

The next banking crisis may not begin with credit losses.

It may begin with the market repricing the durability of banks' future earnings.

AI doesn't need to fail for the Legacy Bubble to burst. It only needs to succeed.

Retail investors are extremely bullish:

Allocation to stocks among retail investors in the AAII survey rose +0.7 percentage points in September, to 71.8%, the highest level since December 2017.

This also marks its 2nd-highest reading since July 2000.

Since April, this figure has risen +3.3 percentage points, its largest 5-month increase since October 2025.

To put this into perspective, average retail exposure to stocks since 1987 is 71.8%.

Meanwhile, allocation to cash fell -1.0 percentage point last month to 13.3%, its lowest since December 2017.

At the same time, allocation to bonds rose +0.3 percentage points, to 14.9%, remaining below its average of 15.9% since 1987.

Appetite for risk among retail investors is through the roof.
